Capacity planning and dedicated pool sizing

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-31
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Aisha (Nimbus Head of ML), Carlos (Platform), Lena (Security), Tom (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — agenda is roll out plan, canary strategy, monitoring and runbooks, and then action items. Anything to add?
[00:14] Tom: Nope that's good. We want to make sure we lock down the rollback steps because last time we had a cascade from a model mismatch.
[00:28] Jonah: Totally. We'll put explicit health checks at the model level and at the request path. We'll also do automatic fallback to the hosted smaller variant if latency spikes.
[00:42] Aisha: Can you say what you mean by fallback? Is that automatic, or do we trigger it?
[00:49] Jonah: There's an automated policy we can enable so if p95 latency goes above threshold for N minutes, traffic moves to the lower-latency compatible model variant. It can be auto or manual — we'll recommend auto for the canary but controlled thresholds.
[01:05] Carlos: For the canary, what's the suggested traffic split cadence? We want to avoid a sudden spike.
[01:12] Maya: Our typical pattern is 5% for 48 hours, validate, then 25% for 72 hours, then 50% for 24-48 hours before full cutover. But we can compress depending on your risk tolerance.
[01:29] Lena: From security we need a defined maintenance window and an IP allowlist window for the Dedicated nodes, plus proof of KMS integration.
[01:38] Jonah: We'll include the exact IP ranges and ephemeral ports in the runbook. KMS is supported — we do envelope encryption and can detail the key rotation cadence.
[01:50] Tom: Great, show me the rollback flow. If during canary error rate spikes we must be able to switch back in under 5 minutes.
[01:58] Jonah: The runbook will have an automated traffic shift (via smart router) plus manual CLI commands to drain instances and flip routing. We test the CLI in the dry-run.
[02:10] Maya: OK let's roll through metrics. What metrics do you want to see in the dashboard?
[02:16] Aisha: Latency at p50/p95, token throughput, model error rate (e.g., API 5xx), quality eval delta on a sampled prompt set, and cost per 1k tokens.
[02:27] Jonah: We'll expose those. We'll also add KV cache hit rate, batch size distribution, and GPU utilization on Dedicated.
[02:36] Carlos: On utilization — how do we size the dedicated pool? We're expecting an initial burst pattern with prolonged tails.
[02:44] Jonah: For burst-friendly workloads we recommend a baseline reserved capacity to cover p95, plus autoscale policies and a small burst buffer (20-30%). We'll include a sizing calc in the doc based on your sample trace.
[02:58] Carlos: We'll upload the trace after the call.
[03:02] Aisha: About A/B testing: we want to A/B prompts and models to see quality delta vs cost. How is that instrumented?
[03:10] Jonah: Redwood Console supports route-level split testing. We can record responses and compute evaluation metrics against your golden set. We'll put the config as part of the canary config so A/B can run concurrently with traffic slices.
[03:24] Maya: Quick note on costs: during the POC you'll see both model compute and token costs; we'll send a simple cost per 1k token sheet tuned to the quantization profile you're using.
[03:34] Tom: Any concerns about data residency or logs? We need audit logs for all inference requests plus KMS access logs.
[03:41] Lena: And retention controls — we can't keep transcribed PII in logs beyond 30 days.
[03:47] Jonah: We can configure retention windows and provide audit logs; for PII we recommend using request-scrubbing or enable redaction rules at the ingress. We'll include that in the security checklist.
[03:59] Maya: Jonah, can you walk through a sample canary runbook outline now?
[04:05] Jonah: Sure. Outline: pre-checks (security checklist, KMS keys, allowlist), initial traffic slice (5%), health metrics to monitor (latency, error rate, quality sample), escalation paths, automated fallback policy, manual rollback commands, and dry-run schedule.
[04:22] Aisha: For the quality sample, we need to ensure it's blind. We have a 250-prompt set. We'll run it against the canary and baseline and look for regressions.
[04:32] Jonah: Perfect, we'll add an eval job that triggers nightly during the canary and posts a summary to the dashboard.
[04:39] Carlos: About monitoring — what alert thresholds do you typically recommend?
[04:45] Jonah: For initial canary: p95 latency > target + 150ms for 5m, error rate > 1% for 5m, quality regression > X% (we'll pick threshold with you). Those can be tuned after the first 48 hours.
[04:59] Aisha: Who gets paged? We need to route pages to Nimbus on-call and Redwood SRE as a backup.
[05:06] Maya: We'll configure escalation: first page Nimbus on-call; if not acknowledged in 10 minutes, Redwood SRE joins. Critical alerts will auto-open the incident channel.
[05:16] Tom: What about observability retention? We might want 90 days for metrics and 1 year for audit logs. Any constraints?
[05:24] Jonah: For metrics we can keep 90 days with detailed retention; logs are available for export and can be kept in your S3 via the Private control plane if needed. There may be additional cost for longer retention — we'll call that out.
[05:36] Maya: Let's talk cutover timing. Are we aiming for a weekend cutover or weekday?
[05:42] Tom: Prefer weekend but willing for weekday off-peak if we can do a dry-run during a weekday.
[05:47] Jonah: We'll schedule a dry-run smoke test on 2026-04-07 (Wednesday) to validate runbooks; final cutover can be weekend 2026-04-11. Put both tentative in calendar.
[05:58] Aisha: Dry-run scope — run the automated traffic shift, execute rollback, and validate alerts. Also we want to test SSO flows and KMS access during the run.
[06:09] Lena: Security will join the dry-run and do a small pen-test of the auth flows.
[06:15] Carlos: For the dry-run, what load should we test? We'll simulate a 2x expected load and 5k qps bursts for 60s.
[06:23] Jonah: That sounds good. We'll provide a load test harness and sample scripts. We'll run it in a staging cluster that mirrors production.
[06:30] Maya: On A/B metrics — Aisha, what's your primary quality metric? Precision? Human eval?
[06:36] Aisha: We'll use a combination: human-rated relevance (1-5), plus automated BLEU-like score against golden answers for structured prompts. We'll compute delta and threshold.
[06:45] Jonah: We'll set the eval job to compute both and surface it in the dashboard.
[06:48] Tom: Anything about RBAC? We need fine-grained roles so only specific apps can call model route.
[06:54] Jonah: Console supports per-route API keys and role-based access; we'll set application-level keys for your services and restrict user-level admin roles.
[07:03] Maya: Quick tangent — competitors. Are you evaluating Anthropic as well?
[07:08] Tom: Yes, still running evals against Anthropic and OpenAI. Cost delta is a big part of our decision.
[07:15] Maya: Understood; we'll make sure our cost/capacity numbers are clear.
[07:19] Jonah: Also note model quantization choices will affect both latency and quality. We'll include recommended quant profiles per model.
[07:29] Carlos: For Dedicated: how are upgrades handled? We need zero-downtime patching.
[07:35] Jonah: Dedicated pools support rolling upgrades with drain and warm-up. We'll document the step-by-step and expected impact.
[07:44] Lena: Audit logs again — we need immutable logs for certain endpoints. Can you sign an appendix?
[07:50] Maya: We'll share the security docs; legal can add an appendix if required.
[07:55] Aisha: Ok to talk about success criteria for the pilot? We need to see 95th percentile latency under 600ms and quality parity within 5% of current baseline, and total cost per 1k tokens less than $X.
[08:08] Maya: We'll map those to the canary pass/fail checks and the A/B analysis.
[08:14] Jonah: Also recommend a burn-in period after cutover where we monitor model drift against the eval set. We'll keep the golden set evaluation running daily for 2 weeks post cutover.
[08:25] Carlos: On incidents — what is the expected MTTR target?
[08:29] Jonah: For infra-related issues we aim for sub-15 minute detection and under 1 hour MTTR for common faults, with rollback within 5 minutes as a hard requirement.
[08:39] Tom: That works.
[08:42] Maya: Anything else? If not, I'll summarize.
[08:46] Jonah: One more — alpha fallback policy: we recommended a smaller model variant that maintains semantics but lowers token cost; ensure your app tolerates small quality deltas.
[08:58] Aisha: We'll validate the tolerance in our A/B.
[09:02] Maya: Summary: canary 5% -> 25% -> 50% with automated fallback, Jonah to prepare runbook and dashboards, Maya to send pricing/SLA, Nimbus to run load tests and security checks, dry-run 2026-04-07, final cutover 2026-04-11.
[09:18] Tom: Good recap.
[09:21] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the documents.
[09:26] Carlos: Thanks.
[09:28] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional word swaps (e.g., KV cache referenced as "K-V' cache"), speaker labels approximate. Links shared: "pilot-pricing.xlsx" (Maya), "canary-runbook-draft.md" (Jonah), "staging-loadtrace-20260331.json" (Carlos).
